facts.title: The Hidden Twin
facts.text: Neodymium's name comes from the Greek for "new twin," because in 1885 the Austrian chemist Carl Auer von Welsbach split a substance previously thought to be a single element, didymium, into two. The pieces became praseodymium ("green twin") and neodymium. Didymium itself had been discovered decades earlier by Carl Mosander, who mistook the mixture for one element.

facts.title: World's Strongest Magnets
facts.text: Neodymium is the key ingredient in Nd2Fe14B, the most powerful type of permanent magnet ever commercialized, developed independently by General Motors and Sumitomo in 1984. These magnets can lift more than a thousand times their own weight, and a small one can pinch skin hard enough to cause injury. They power earbuds, hard drives, wind-turbine generators, and the motors of nearly every electric vehicle.

facts.title: A Color-Changing Crystal
facts.text: Glass and crystals doped with neodymium ions display a striking property called alexandrite-like dichroism, appearing lavender or pale blue under daylight but warm pink or violet under incandescent or fluorescent light. This happens because the Nd ion absorbs narrow bands of yellow light, and the leftover color depends on the lamp's spectrum. Jewelers and glassmakers prize this effect in "neodymium glass."

facts.title: Light Powerful Enough to Fuse Atoms
facts.text: Neodymium-doped yttrium aluminium garnet (Nd:YAG) is one of the most widely used laser materials in the world, emitting infrared light at 1064 nanometers. Nd:glass lasers drive the giant National Ignition Facility in California, which in 2022 achieved the first laser fusion reaction to release more energy than the lasers delivered. The same family of lasers also cuts steel, marks metal, and performs eye and skin surgery.

facts.title: Not So Rare After All
facts.text: Despite being a "rare earth," neodymium is fairly common in the crust at about 38 parts per million, making it more abundant than gold, silver, or even lead. The challenge is that it never occurs as a pure metal in nature and is always thinly spread among other lanthanides in minerals like monazite and bastnasite. Separating the chemically near-identical rare earths is the truly difficult and costly part.

facts.title: It Tarnishes Fast
facts.text: Pure neodymium metal is silvery and lustrous when freshly cut, but it oxidizes rapidly in air, developing a yellowish crust within hours and flaking away over time. For this reason the metal is usually stored under mineral oil or sealed in plastic. It is also quite reactive with water, slowly producing hydrogen gas.

facts.title: Magnetism Born of Cold
facts.text: Neodymium has unusually complex magnetic behavior of its own: it becomes antiferromagnetic only when chilled below about 20 kelvin, near minus 253 degrees Celsius. In 2018 physicists discovered it can form a "self-induced spin glass," a state where its atomic magnetic moments freeze into a tangled, ever-shifting pattern without any added impurities. This was a surprising find in a supposedly well-understood element.

facts.title: China's Strategic Grip
facts.text: Roughly 60 to 70 percent of the world's neodymium is mined in China, with the giant Bayan Obo deposit in Inner Mongolia being the single largest source. Because the metal is essential to electric motors, wind turbines, and defense systems, governments now treat it as a critical strategic material. Efforts to recycle neodymium from old hard drives and to reopen mines elsewhere, such as Mountain Pass in California, aim to diversify supply.

facts.title: Made in Dying Stars
facts.text: Neodymium, like other lanthanides, is forged in the cosmos mainly through neutron-capture processes inside aging stars and during cataclysmic events such as neutron-star mergers. Astronomers detect its spectral fingerprint in the atmospheres of certain chemically peculiar stars. Every neodymium atom in a magnet on Earth was created in stellar nuclear reactions billions of years before the Sun formed.

facts.title: A Clock in the Rocks
facts.text: The radioactive decay of samarium-147 into neodymium-143 gives geologists the samarium-neodymium dating method, capable of measuring the ages of rocks over billions of years. By comparing neodymium isotope ratios, scientists have dated some of Earth's oldest crust and even meteorites from the early Solar System. Neodymium isotopes in deep-sea sediments also help reconstruct how ancient ocean currents flowed.
